expansion point.d: The one input where a Taylor approximation is built: the place where you know the value and the derivatives. The approximation is best there and gets worse as you move away, like a weather forecast that is good for the next hour and poor for next week.

factorial.d: n! (read “n factorial”) is 1 × 2 × … × n, with 0! = 1. So 3! = 6 and 5! = 120. It appears in Taylor approximations because differentiating Δxⁿ n times gives n!.

radius of convergence.d: How far from the expansion point adding more Taylor terms keeps improving the approximation. For ln(1 + x) built at 0 it is 1: at x = 2, more terms make the answer worse, not better.

log-log plot.d: A graph with the logarithm of each quantity on both axes. A power law, error = C × Δxᵏ, becomes a straight line whose slope is k, so you can read the order of an error off the steepness.

natural move size.d: The size of the changes that actually happen in a problem, for example one standard deviation (1σ) of an activation across texts. A model built from derivatives at one point is only trustworthy if the curvature changes little over this distance.

gate.d: A smooth switch: a function that goes from about 0 (off) to about 1 (on) over a short range of its input, like a dimmer that is mostly off, then quickly mostly on. The sigmoid is the standard example. Neural networks contain many of them.

sine.d: sin x: the height of a point that has gone x radians round a circle of radius 1. It wiggles between −1 and 1 forever, repeating every 2π ≈ 6.28 radians.

radian.d: The natural unit of angle: the angle at which the arc of a circle equals its radius. A full turn is 2π ≈ 6.28 radians, so 1 radian ≈ 57.3°.
